alt: A time axis from 700 to 1900. Bars show the lives of al-Ghazali (1058–1111), Ahmad Sirhindi (1564–1624), Shah Waliullah (1703–1762) and Syed Ahmad Barelvi (1786–1831). Markers show Muhammad bin Qasim’s conquest of Sindh in 711–712, Aurangzeb’s death in 1707, Panipat in 1761, Balakot in 1831 and the founding of Deoband in 1867.
caption: Over a thousand years separate Muhammad bin Qasim from the reformers of the 18th and 19th centuries.

after: ## What is Sufism and why did it matter in the subcontinent?
alt: A master (pir or shaikh) with disciples (murids) around him, organised in orders called silsilas and meeting at lodges called khanqahs. A table names Ali Hujwiri of Lahore, Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer (Chishti order) and Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan (Suhrawardi order), with the Qadiri and Naqshbandi orders spreading later.
caption: Sufi orders linked master and disciples, and their khanqahs welcomed everyone.

after: ## What was the importance of Muhammad bin Qasim?
alt: A chain: the Umayyad governor Hajjaj bin Yusuf sends Muhammad bin Qasim to Sindh; in 711–712 he captures Debal and defeats Raja Dahir, bringing Sindh and southern Punjab including Multan under Muslim rule. Four religious impacts follow, which is why Sindh is called Bab-ul-Islam, the gateway of Islam.
caption: The conquest of Sindh made it the gateway of Islam in the subcontinent.

alt: Two boxes, correct practice under the Sharia and inner sincerity, combine into true faith, al-Ghazali’s argument in The Revival of the Religious Sciences. Three effects follow: Sufism brought into mainstream Sunni Islam, criticism of philosophers who put reason above revelation, and lasting influence on madrasas and Sufi orders in the subcontinent.
caption: al-Ghazali joined law and spirituality, a model later scholars followed.

alt: A timeline of Ahmad Sirhindi: born in Sirhind in 1564, he opposed Akbar’s Din-i-Ilahi, wrote hundreds of letters urging orthodox practice, was imprisoned by Jahangir in Gwalior fort and released, and died in 1624. His influence is linked to Aurangzeb’s more orthodox policies and the Fatawa-e-Alamgiri.
caption: Sirhindi insisted Sufism follow the Sharia, shaping orthodoxy under Aurangzeb.

alt: Four problems facing Muslims after 1707 are matched to Shah Waliullah’s responses: political decline to letters urging rulers such as Ahmad Shah Abdali to act; lack of access to the Arabic Qur’an to his Persian translation; Sunni–Shia division to efforts at reconciliation; and tension between law and popular custom to his stress on Sharia, hadith and Hujjat Allah al-Baligha.
caption: Each of Shah Waliullah’s reforms answered a specific cause of Muslim weakness.

after: ## Who was Syed Ahmad Barelvi and what did his Jihad movement achieve?
alt: A timeline: Syed Ahmad Barelvi, born at Rae Bareli in 1786, studied under Shah Abdul Aziz and served with Amir Khan; he preached the Tariqa-i-Muhammadiya; from 1826 he and Shah Ismail Shaheed fought Sikh rule; they held Peshawar briefly in 1830 but were weakened and killed at Balakot in 1831.
caption: The jihad won early battles but local rivalries and Sikh strength ended it at Balakot.

after: ## Who was Syed Ahmad Barelvi and what did his Jihad movement achieve?
alt: A family chart: Shah Abdur Rahim, founder of the Madrasa Rahimiya, is father of Shah Waliullah, whose son Shah Abdul Aziz taught Syed Ahmad Barelvi and whose grandson Shah Ismail Shaheed fought alongside Barelvi from 1826. The movement later influenced the Ahl-i-Hadith and the Deobandi movement founded in 1867.
caption: Shah Waliullah’s family and students carried his reforms into the 19th century.
